newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Shell shares slip, profit disappoints.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Shell shares slip, profit disappoints.

text.p: Royal Dutch/Shell Group on Thursday reported lower second-quarter results, which came as a cold shower after a spate of strong performances from other oil majors.
Shell blamed its chemicals sector, while also pointing at the pound's strength and inventory losses as reasons for not meeting market forecasts.
The Anglo-Dutch group turned in net earnings of 1.140 billion pounds ($1.8 billion), four percent down from 1.187 billion a year ago, while a profit rise had been expected.
Shell shares dropped 15 pence to 458p in London while in Amsterdam, shares in the Dutch arm, Royal Dutch Petroleum, fell 2.30 guilders to 117.90.

Analysts cut their profit estimates and downgraded Shell shares, saying the oil giant was underperforming its main rivals such as British Petroleum in Europe and Mobil Corp and Exxon Corp in the United States.
"They are at the bottom of their peer group," said Irene Himona at broker SocGen, who put Shell on her "sell" list.
Shell said its results were hit by currency losses of 117 million pounds. This was due to sterling's strength in the second quarter, which masked an underlying three percent profit rise.
Higher production offset lower crude oil prices, while chemical earnings were slightly down in the quarter, Shell said.
Chairman Mark Moody-Stuart said the chemicals' sector performance was "disappointing", but he was optimistic for the 1997 second half as a major restructuring programme continued.
"I am confident that by the end of the year we will be ahead of our original road map targets," he said.
Chemicals profits fell one percent in the second quarter due to one-off items such as plant start-up costs in Singapore, Moody-Stuart said.
Another negative "blip" was the fact Shell took 70 percent of its plant maintenance costs in the three months to June 30, he added.
Shell's refining and marketing margins were up 17 percent in the quarter on a current cost basis, but reported earnings were lower because of inventory holding losses.
Crude oil prices in the first half were $1.50 a barrel below a year earlier due to resumption of exports from Iraq and increased non-OPEC production.
The oil price decline as well as lower gas sales resulted in a 10 percent decline in exploration and production profits.
Shell said the outlook was for continued increases in crude oil supply from the North Sea and ample supply of oil products.
It added capital expenditure was set to step up in the second half, after a 16 percent decline to 1.7 billion pounds in the year to June 30.
Paradoxically, some leading analysts said this drop showed Shell was spending its money more wisely and saw it as evidence of strong growth ahead.
"Clearly the drive to improve returns in downstream and chemicals is not yet evident," said Fergus Macleod at NatWest Markets said.
"But the fact Shell is undershooting its capital budget is clear evidence pressure is mounting on the operational management for better results," he added. ($ = 0.624 British Pounds)
